Model and assumptions. Use b₂ → 10 kΩ (MSB), b₁ → 20 kΩ, and b₀ → 40 kΩ (LSB). This mapping is an explicit assumption based on the supplied description. The high level VH and actual supply rails are unknown, so the core derivation stays symbolic. Tables use VH = 5 V as an illustrative assumption. The image available to embed in the current library is a different 4-bit BCD reference drawing, not a screenshot showing −15.001 V; it is embedded unchanged and this mismatch is disclosed below rather than misrepresented. The simulator used was not specified, so the lesson is simulator-neutral and does not claim a real Multisim or Falstad run.

1. Introduction and learning objectives

A digital-to-analog converter (DAC) maps a digital code into a corresponding analog voltage or current. A binary-weighted DAC uses differently valued resistors to give each bit a different contribution. Here an inverting op-amp sums those currents and produces a negative output.

By the end, you can…

  • Derive the output from virtual ground, Ohm’s law and KCL.
  • Calculate all eight output levels and the LSB step.
  • Predict clipping/saturation and investigate a suspicious reading.
  • Compare weighted-resistor and R–2R DACs.
  • Answer exam, GATE-style and interview questions.

Prerequisites

  • Ideal inverting amplifier
  • Virtual ground and negative feedback
  • Ohm’s law and Kirchhoff’s current law
  • Binary numbers and superposition

Why DACs matter

Audio playback, waveform generators, instrumentation, programmable references, actuator control and embedded systems all use digital values to control real-world analog signals.

Terminology

TermMeaning
MSB / LSBMost / least significant bit. For this assumed mapping, b₂ has weight 4 and b₀ weight 1.
ResolutionSmallest nominal code increment; for N bits there are 2ᴺ codes.
LSB stepMagnitude of the voltage change for one code count.
Full-scale outputOutput at the largest code, here 111. This is not always the same as a convention that defines full-scale range as 2ᴺ LSBs.
MonotonicityOutput changes consistently in one direction as code increases.
Settling timeTime for output to enter and remain within a specified error band after a code change.
INL / DNLIntegral nonlinearity: deviation from a reference transfer line. Differential nonlinearity: each code step’s deviation from one ideal LSB.

DAC families

Binary-weighted resistor, R–2R ladder, current-steering and sigma-delta DACs. They trade resistor complexity, speed, resolution, noise and filtering requirements differently.

3. Working principle

  1. Set the bits. A bit bᵢ is 0 or 1. Its ideal source voltage is bᵢVH.
  2. Virtual ground. With negative feedback and linear operation, the op-amp drives its output so the inverting node is approximately 0 V because the non-inverting input is grounded. The node is not physically connected to ground.
  3. Branch currents. By Ohm’s law, I₂ = b₂VH/10 kΩ, I₁ = b₁VH/20 kΩ and I₀ = b₀VH/40 kΩ.
  4. KCL. Ideal op-amp input current is approximately zero, so the three branch currents add and flow through Rf.
  5. Feedback conversion. Vout = −Rf(I₂ + I₁ + I₀). The negative sign comes from the inverting summing amplifier.
  6. Check headroom. If the calculated output magnitude exceeds the op-amp’s available output swing, the ideal linear equation no longer predicts the actual output. The output clips near a rail, usually before reaching the supply voltage exactly.

Why R, 2R, 4R?

For the same input voltage, current is inversely proportional to resistance. Therefore 10 kΩ, 20 kΩ and 40 kΩ create current weights in the ratio 4:2:1. The MSB has the smallest resistor and the largest contribution.

Ideal assumptions

Infinite open-loop gain, infinite input impedance, zero input offset, sufficient bandwidth/slew rate, ideal logic levels, negligible source resistance and operation within output swing.

Practical checks

Resistor tolerance/matching, op-amp input offset and bias current, source loading, reference stability, output swing, bandwidth, slew rate, settling, noise and PCB leakage.

Common misconceptions

  • “The output should be positive.” Not with this inverting topology and positive input levels: Vout is negative.
  • “The MSB uses the largest resistor.” No. It uses the smallest resistor, so it contributes the largest current.
  • “Virtual ground is a real ground wire.” No. It is a feedback-maintained approximate voltage.
  • “An ideal calculation can exceed the rails.” The equation is a linear-region model. Physical output saturates/clips.
  • “All resistor tolerances matter equally.” Absolute error impact depends on branch weight; MSB branch accuracy often matters most.

A second inverting stage can restore positive polarity. Alternatively, use a different reference/topology designed for a positive output.

4. Equations and derivation

Step 1: branch currents

I₂ = b₂V_H / 10 kΩ; I₁ = b₁V_H / 20 kΩ; I₀ = b₀V_H / 40 kΩ

Step 2: apply KCL and feedback

I_total = V_H (b₂/10k + b₁/20k + b₀/40k)
Vout = −Rf · I_total

For Rf = 5 kΩ, convert the conductance weights to the same denominator:

Vout = −5k · V_H (b₂/10k + b₁/20k + b₀/40k)
= −V_H (0.5b₂ + 0.25b₁ + 0.125b₀)
= −V_H(4b₂ + 2b₁ + b₀)/8

Here b₂, b₁, b₀ are dimensionless bits (0 or 1); VH is volts; resistors are ohms; current is amperes; Vout is volts.

General N-bit weighted DAC

For an N-bit input dN−1…d₀, choose Ri = 2N−1−iR for bit i, with MSB resistor R and feedback Rf:

Vout = −(Rf/R) V_H Σ[i=0 to N−1] d_i / 2^(N−1−i)

Equivalently, if D = Σ dᵢ2ⁱ is the unsigned code and Rf/R = 1/2 for the 3-bit example’s scaling, Vout = −VHD/2ᴺ. The 3-bit specific form is −VHD/8.

Resolution, step and full scale

LSB step magnitude = (Rf/R_MSB) · V_H / 2^(N−1)

For this 3-bit circuit, Rf/RMSB = 5k/10k = 0.5, hence ΔV = VH/8. Under the stated code convention:

Vout(D) = −V_H D/8; D = 0…7
Vout(000) = 0 V; Vout(111) = −7V_H/8

For VH = 5 V, ΔV = 0.625 V and the full-scale code output is −4.375 V. Resolution as a fraction of the endpoint full-scale magnitude is 1/(2ᴺ−1); as a percent, 100/(2ᴺ−1)%. Note that the code step based on a 2ᴺ denominator is often quoted as 1/2ᴺ of the reference scale, so state the convention.

Changing Rf and tolerance

All output levels scale linearly with Rf while the op-amp remains in its linear region. A fractional change ε in Rf scales all levels by approximately ε. A fractional error ε₂ in the 10 kΩ MSB resistor changes that branch current by approximately −ε₂ for small errors because I = V/R; this produces the largest single-bit weighted error for a given fractional resistor error.

Limiting cases

  • All zeros: no ideal input current, so Vout = 0 V (ignoring offset/bias/leakage).
  • All ones: summed current is maximum, so Vout = −7VH/8 for this 3-bit scaling.
  • Beyond available output swing: the op-amp saturates and output no longer follows the ideal formula.

Physical meaning: each bit adds a fixed weighted current. More code bits set to 1 make the output more negative; one code increment changes the ideal output by one LSB step.

Interpreting the stated −15.001 V reading

For code 111 and the illustrative assumption VH = 5 V, the ideal prediction is:

Vout = −(5 V)(4+2+1)/8 = −4.375 V

To obtain −15.001 V from the ideal equation at code 111, the required logic-high level would be:

−15.001 V = −7V_H/8 ⇒ V_H = 15.001 × 8/7 ≈ 17.144 V

So the reading is far from the 5 V example. It is most consistent with output saturation near a ±15 V supply rail, or with a different logic-high level, among other possible setup issues. These are possible explanations only; the actual logic-high setting and op-amp supply voltages are not visible in the described screenshot, so the cause cannot be determined from the reading alone. A display of −15.001 V does not prove the rail voltage or the exact logic level.

How to verify

  • Check the digital source’s logic-high voltage setting VH.
  • Check the op-amp positive and negative supply rails and the selected op-amp model’s output swing.
  • Verify Rf = 5 kΩ, the feedback path, common summing node and input resistor mapping.
  • Confirm the 10 kΩ branch is b₂ (MSB), 20 kΩ is b₁ and 40 kΩ is b₀ under the stated assumption.
  • Re-run all eight input combinations and record the measured output.

Theoretical staircase, VH = 5 V

7. Solved numerical problems

Problem 1 · Output for a code

Given: Rf = 5 kΩ, input resistors 10 kΩ / 20 kΩ / 40 kΩ, VH = 5 V (assumed), code 101. Required: Vout.

Formula: Vout = −VH(4b₂ + 2b₁ + b₀)/8.

Substitution: b₂ = 1, b₁ = 0, b₀ = 1, so Vout = −(5 V)(4+0+1)/8 = −25/8 V = −3.125 V.

Final answer: −3.125 V. Interpretation: both the MSB and LSB current contributions add at the inverting node. Shortcut: convert 101₂ to decimal 5 and calculate −5×5/8.

Problem 2 · Choose Rf for 0 to −10 V at full scale

Given: same input resistors and VH = 5 V, full-scale code 111. Required: feedback resistance for Vout = −10 V ideally.

Formula: at 111, Itotal = 5/10k + 5/20k + 5/40k = 0.5 mA + 0.25 mA + 0.125 mA = 0.875 mA. Vout = −Rf Itotal.

Substitution: Rf = 10 V / 0.875 mA = 11.4286 kΩ.

Final answer: Rf ≈ 11.43 kΩ. Interpretation: the ideal endpoint becomes −10 V, but the op-amp must have sufficient negative output swing and the chosen resistor value must be practical. Shortcut: Rf = 10 V ÷ 0.875 mA.

Problem 3 · GATE-style 5-bit extension

Given: N = 5 bits, VH = 3.3 V, MSB input resistor R = 10 kΩ, Rf = 5 kΩ and binary-weighted resistors R, 2R, 4R, 8R, 16R. Required: LSB step and full-scale output magnitude.

Formula: ΔV = (Rf/R)VH/2N−1; FS magnitude = (2N−1)ΔV.

Substitution: ΔV = (0.5)(3.3 V)/16 = 0.103125 V. FS = 31×0.103125 V = 3.196875 V.

Final answer: LSB = 103.125 mV; Vout(FS) = −3.196875 V. Interpretation: the output remains negative. Shortcut: multiply the step by 31 for a 5-bit endpoint.

Problem 4 · Investigate the stated screenshot reading

Given: code 111, reading stated as −15.001 V; reference case assumes VH = 5 V. Required: compare theory and infer the VH needed by the ideal formula.

Theory: Vout = −5×7/8 = −4.375 V.

Required high level: VH = 8×15.001/7 = 17.144 V approximately.

Final interpretation: −15.001 V is not consistent with the 5 V ideal example. It may indicate saturation near a negative rail or a different logic-high level, but the prompt does not reveal the actual VH or supply rails. Check settings and all codes before deciding.

Problem 5 · MSB resistor tolerance

Given: 10 kΩ MSB resistor is 1% high, b₂ = 1, other bits 0, VH = 5 V, Rf = 5 kΩ. Required: actual MSB-only output.

Actual resistor = 10.1 kΩ. Current = 5/10.1k = 0.49505 mA. Output = −5k × 0.49505 mA = −2.47525 V. Ideal MSB-only output = −2.5 V.

Final answer: about −2.475 V, a +24.75 mV deviation (less negative). The 1% larger resistor reduces current by approximately 1%; for the MSB, that error affects a large code weight.

8. GATE preparation · 10 original MCQs

These are original practice questions, not claimed previous-year questions. Choose an option to reveal the answer and reasoning.

9. Core electronics interview preparation

Expand each prompt to review a concise answer and a useful follow-up point.

1. Why is the R–2R ladder preferred to a binary-weighted resistor DAC?

It uses only two resistor values, R and 2R, so matching and integrated-circuit layout are easier. A binary-weighted network needs a wide range of accurate values as resolution increases.

Follow-up: R–2R still depends on resistor ratio matching, switch resistance and reference quality.

2. What limits DAC accuracy?

Resistor/reference tolerances, op-amp offset and bias currents, finite gain, noise, switch resistance, loading, temperature drift, quantization, INL and DNL all contribute.

Follow-up: separate static errors (offset, gain, INL/DNL) from dynamic behavior (glitch, settling, slew rate).

3. What do you check if output is stuck near a rail?

Confirm supply rails and common ground, input logic levels, resistor values and mapping, feedback continuity, op-amp pinout, output load and whether the ideal output exceeds available swing.

Follow-up: test 000 first, then one bit at a time, then all ones.

4. How does bandwidth affect settling?

Finite closed-loop bandwidth slows response after code changes. Slew-rate limiting can dominate for large steps; settling time includes the time to enter and remain within a specified error band.

5. How would you test monotonicity?

Apply codes in increasing order and measure output after settling. For this inverting circuit, each next code should be no more positive than the previous one, with nominal change −1 LSB. Check that no step reverses direction.

6. Why is the output negative?

The circuit is an inverting summing amplifier. Positive input currents flow into the virtual-ground node, and the op-amp drives negative to provide feedback current through Rf.

7. What is virtual ground, and when does it fail?

Negative feedback and high open-loop gain make the inverting node approximately equal to the grounded non-inverting input. It fails as a useful approximation when the amplifier saturates, feedback opens or bandwidth is inadequate.

8. How do you verify the MSB and LSB mapping?

Activate each bit separately and compare magnitudes. With 5 V and this scaling, b₂ alone gives −2.5 V, b₁ alone −1.25 V, and b₀ alone −0.625 V. Do not infer the mapping solely from wire positions.

9. What is a glitch in a DAC?

A brief transient during a code transition, often because switches do not change simultaneously. It can be important in fast waveform generation even if the final static code is accurate.

10. How do you measure INL and DNL?

Measure output at each code after settling. DNL compares each code step with one ideal LSB. INL compares each measured point with a defined ideal endpoint or best-fit line; the convention must be stated.

11. What simulation mistakes are common?

Wrong op-amp supply pins, unpowered op-amp, floating grounds, wrong resistor units, nonideal digital high levels, incorrect feedback node, and reading output before settling.

12. How would you improve the circuit for a positive output?

Add a second unity-gain inverting stage if suitable, or choose a reference/topology that yields the required polarity. Re-check range, headroom, offsets and loading after the change.

Industry perspective: Analog/mixed-signal engineers care about transfer accuracy, reference integrity, noise, layout and corner cases. Hardware validation engineers create repeatable code sweeps, automate measurements and compare bench data with expected limits. Embedded engineers coordinate DAC updates with timers, DMA, firmware interfaces and output filtering. Being able to explain both the ideal equation and why the bench measurement differs is valuable.

10. Applications and industry relevance

Audio playback

Digital samples become analog waveforms. High-resolution commercial audio typically uses more sophisticated architectures and filtering than a three-bit teaching circuit.

Waveform/function generators

Code sequences form ramps, steps and approximations to periodic signals.

Programmable voltage sources

Set thresholds, bias points and calibration levels.

Motor and actuator control

Generate analog command references for downstream drivers or controllers.

Test and measurement

Stimulus generation, calibration and automated validation.

Microcontroller analog outputs

Some MCUs contain DAC peripherals; others approximate analog output with PWM plus a low-pass filter.

Typical implementation challenges

  • Resistor matching and reference drift
  • Switching glitches, noise and ground bounce
  • Output loading and op-amp drive capability
  • Settling time, bandwidth and slew-rate limits
  • Calibration across temperature and production spread

Related roles: analog design engineer, mixed-signal IC engineer, validation/test engineer, hardware design engineer, applications engineer and embedded systems engineer.

12. Revision materials

Formula sheet

Vout = −Rf Σ(V_i/R_i)
3-bit circuit: Vout = −V_H(4b₂ + 2b₁ + b₀)/8
Code D = 4b₂ + 2b₁ + b₀
Vout(D) = −V_HD/8
LSB step magnitude = V_H/8 (for Rf = 5 kΩ, R_MSB = 10 kΩ)
Full-scale endpoint = −7V_H/8
V_H required for target |V_FS| = 8|V_FS|/7

High-priority exam points

  • Use KCL at the virtual-ground summing node.
  • Remember the negative sign of an inverting summer.
  • For VH = 5 V: step = 0.625 V; 111 gives −4.375 V.
  • Output saturation invalidates the ideal linear prediction.
  • R–2R reduces the number of distinct resistor values to two.
  • Monotonicity is about correct direction; INL and DNL quantify different errors.

Advantages and disadvantages

Advantages
  • Simple, intuitive circuit
  • Fast concept demonstration
  • Direct current summation
  • Easy hand calculations for low bit counts
Disadvantages
  • Wide resistor spread as bit count rises
  • Accuracy depends on resistor tolerance and source levels
  • Logic sources can be loaded
  • Op-amp offset, bandwidth and output swing matter
  • High-resolution implementation is awkward, so R–2R is often preferred

Architecture comparison

ArchitectureStrengthsTrade-offs / typical notes
Binary-weighted resistorSimple and intuitiveWide resistor range; source loading and matching issues
R–2R ladderOnly R and 2R values; scalable layoutSwitch resistance and ratio matching still matter
Current-steeringCan be very fast; common in high-speed DACsCurrent-source matching, glitch and layout complexity
Sigma-deltaHigh resolution with oversampling/noise shapingNeeds digital processing and output filtering; often lower bandwidth than high-speed current-steering

Troubleshooting quick list

  • Output near zero: check bits, source levels, common ground, feedback and meter reference.
  • Output stuck at negative rail: check requested code, VH, Rf, supply pins and output swing.
  • Wrong step size: verify resistor values and Rf, then calculate actual VH.
  • Nonuniform steps: check resistor tolerance, source impedance, loading and op-amp nonidealities.
  • Noisy or unstable output: inspect grounding, decoupling, wiring, load capacitance and bandwidth/compensation.

Memory aid: “Small R, Strong bit; currents Add; Inverting means minus; Rails rule.”
